COURT FILE NO.:
06-CV-312373
PD2

DATE:
2009/07/21

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE - ONTARIO

RE:
GUNNAR
S. PAULSSON v. LEO COOPER, THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF AND FOR THE UNIVERSITY OF ILLINOIS,
THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION FOR THE ADVANCEMENT OF SLAVIC STUDIES, and SLAVIC
REVIEW

BEFORE:
Moore J.

COUNSEL:
Geoffrey
Adair, Q.C. and Agape Lim, for the Defendants/Applicants

David
Brooker and Anton Pribetic, for the Plaintiff/Respondent

E N D O R S E M E N T

[
1
]

The
defendants (except Leo Cooper) seek an order setting aside service
ex juris
upon
them or, in the alternative, staying this action. The contention is three
pronged: there is no real and substantial connection between the subject matter
of the proceeding and the Province of Ontario; and, in any event, Ontario is
not a convenient forum for the hearing of the proceeding. The third assertion
is that one applicant is entitled to shelter under immunity provisions enacted
under the
State Immunity Act.

Background

[
2
]

This action
arises out of the publication of an allegedly defamatory book review in the
June 2004 issue of an academic journal,
The Slavic Review.
The subject
of the book review, authored by Dr. Leo Cooper, was a book authored by the
plaintiff and entitled
Secret City: the Hidden Jews of Warsaw, 1940-1945.

[
3
]

The
plaintiff (“Paulsson”) is a resident of Ontario and, but for a period of about
ten years during which he studied and worked abroad, he has lived in Ontario
since 1958.

[
4
]

He studied
at the University of Oxford and, at age 51, he obtained a doctoral degree,
granted in 1998. His specialty is the Holocaust in Poland and that intersects
three subjects, the Holocaust and genocide studies, Polish history and Eastern
European Jewish history.

[
5
]

Paulsson
attended Oxford on a Commonwealth Scholarship. He also taught at the University
of Leicester in England and later at Oxford and he wrote several articles. He worked
at the Imperial War Museum in London, England and on a post graduate fellowship
at the U.S. Holocaust Museum in Washington, D.C.. He returned to Canada in 2002
and has sought out tenure track teaching opportunities, so far without success,
ever since.

[
6
]

To earn
income, he has worked as a telemarketer and by writing resumes, cover letters, business
letters and by revising two doctoral dissertations for students; he accepted
brief contract positions, including a part time teaching engagement in Germany.

[
7
]

Paulsson believes
he is quite well known within the Polish studies community worldwide. He
received the Polish Studies Association prize in 2004.

[
8
]

His book
was published in 2002; it was released in Britain in January 2003 and on this
side of the Atlantic in March of 2003. This period approximated the fifth year
after Paulsson had completed his graduate studies. Normally, five years is the
horizon for post doctoral fellowships. He was expecting and hoping that the
book would “turn the corner” for him and propel him into a career in academia.
That didn’t happen.

[
9
]

Three
thousand copies of the book have been printed. 1300 sold in the first year and
sales have been hovering at just under 100 per year since.

[
10
]

The amended statement of claim
asserts that Paulsson was defamed in a book review written by the defendant,
Dr. Leo Cooper (“Cooper”), an Australian resident and senior fellow of the
Contemporary Europe Research Center at the University of Melbourne, Australia.

[
11
]

Cooper allegedly fabricated
quotations which were stated to be taken from Paulsson’s book, took other
quotations out of context and he chose not to refer to various other
information in the book which would have contradicted statements made in Cooper’s
book review. The claim further alleges that certain statements are false and
defamatory and were written with Cooper's knowledge or without regard to the
truthfulness of the statements.

[
12
]

Paulsson maintains that the
defamatory nature of the book review at issue in this case has contributed to
the fact that he has been rejected as a candidate for academic jobs in Canada
and elsewhere although he admits that since June 2004 the subject of the book review
has not been raised in the course of any job application or interview and much
the same criticism as he points to as defamatory in this case has been
published by a man who is the chair of the history department at the University
of Ottawa. As well, he testified that he believes his age, now more than 62
years, has adversely affected his efforts to secure an academic or teaching
career, both before and after the publication of the book review.

[
13
]

Paulsson asserts that for an
academic who lacks the protection of a tenured post, his reputation is his only
valuable possession but there is precious little evidence available on this
application to describe Paulsson’s reputation in Ontario generally or the
nature and extent of the impression upon it worked by the publication of his
book and/or of any negative review of the book.

[
14
]

Cooper has not defended this
action and pleadings against him have been noted in default. Cooper wrote his
book review on Paulsson’s book in June 2004. Reference to the review was
pre-published in the Melbourne Holocaust Studies Centre Newsletter where a
friend read it and brought it to Paulsson’s attention.

[
15
]

The review was then published in
the Slavic Review in June 2004. Paulsson has no knowledge of where in Ontario
the Slavic Review was available in 2004 but he did an investigation in 2008 and
counted some 24 libraries that carry it. There is no evidence that anyone in
Ontario actually read the Cooper review.

[
16
]

The American Association for the
Advancement of Slavic Studies (“the Association”) published the Slavic Review.

[
17
]

The Association is a nonprofit
corporation, incorporated in New York State. Its objective is to represent
American scholarship in the post Soviet/East Central European field nationally
and internationally. Its national office is located in Massachusetts. It does
not own any property or transact any business in the province of Ontario.

[
18
]

The Slavic Review is an
international interdisciplinary academic journal focused on the study of
Eastern Europe, Russia, the Caucasus and Central Asia.

[
19
]

After the Cooper review was
published in the June 2004 issue of the Slavic Review, 81 copies or 2.4% of the
total copies distributed of that issue were distributed in Ontario. The issue
was not available for purchase on newsstands and back issues are available for
purchase only through the Association.

[
20
]

The June 2004 issue of the Slavic
Review containing the book review at issue in this matter was never and is not
available in electronic form from the Slavic Review’s website or the
Association's website. Only issues published from 2006 onwards are available in
electronic form on the Association's website and only to members of the
Association.

[
21
]

The evidence on this application
establishes that the only way for the public to access the June 2004 issue
electronically is through JSTOR, a digital archive of scholarly works. The
issue would have been available online on JSTOR sometime in 2005.

[
22
]

The University of Illinois (“the
University”) provides certain support to the Slavic Review by reason of the
fact that it is the home institution of the scholar, Prof. Mark Steinberg, who
is editor of the Slavic Review.

[
23
]

The University does not publish
the Slavic Review, nor did it have any control or authority over the Slavic
Review or contribute in any way to editorial decisions on content.

[
24
]

The University does not own
property or transact any business in the province of Ontario.

[
25
]

Paulsson has testified that he
does not believe any witnesses are needed in this case on the liability issue.
He may retain, but has not yet retained, and accounting expert to opine on
damages issues. He may call one or two doctors to address damages issues as
well.

[
26
]

The defendants have identified
several possible witnesses, all of whom reside outside of Ontario.

[
27
]

The
University Of Illinois Act
[1]

requires that claims in tort against the Board of Trustees must be filed in
the Illinois Court of Claims, a quasi judicial body that hears claims against
state agencies or state employees and that may award damages in amounts not to
exceed $100,000.00 to or for the benefit of any claimant.
[2]

Issues

[
28
]

The applicants raise the following
3 issues for determination on this application:

(a)

Does this court have jurisdiction on the basis that there is a real and
substantial connection between Ontario and the litigation?

(b)

If this court has jurisdiction, should it exercise discretion and
decline to assume jurisdiction because Ontario is not the most convenient
forum?

(c)

Does the university enjoy sovereign immunity pursuant to

the

State Immunity Act?
[3]

[
29
]

The parties agree that into the
appropriate mix of factors important in determining whether litigation has a
real and substantial connection to Ontario, these factors must be considered
and no one factor is determinative:

•

the connection between the forum and the plaintiffs claim;

•

the connection between the forum and the defendants;

•

unfairness to the defendants in assuming jurisdiction;

•

unfairness to the plaintiff in not assuming jurisdiction;

•

the involvement of other parties to the suit;

•

the courts willingness to recognize and enforce an extra-provincial
judgment rendered on the same jurisdictional basis;

•

whether the case is inter-provincial or international in nature;
and

•

comity and the standards of jurisdiction, recognition and
enforcement prevailing elsewhere.
[4]

The Connection Between Ontario and the
Plaintiff’s Case

[
30
]

Paulsson submits that in a claim
in libel, the tort of defamation is committed where the publication takes place
and that is where the offending words were heard, read or downloaded and if the
alleged defamatory statements were published or republished in Ontario and are
alleged to have caused injury in Ontario, then the connection between the
subject matter of the actions and Ontario is significant.

[
31
]

The applicants do not disagree
with the characterization of the test but assert that its application to a
particular case must be made with a considerable measure of judgment.
Skywriting of defamatory words above remote regions of Antarctica is very
different than publication of those words about a prominent citizen in national
newspapers with enormous readership in Ontario.
[5]

[
32
]

In
Muscutt
, Sharpe J.A.
admonished that:

… if the plaintiff lacks a significant connection
with the forum, the case for assuming jurisdiction on the basis of damage
sustained within the jurisdiction is weaker. If the connection is tenuous,
courts should be wary of assuming jurisdiction. Mere residence in the
jurisdiction does not constitute a sufficient basis for assuming jurisdiction.
[6]

[
33
]

The applicants add that the
distribution of the Cooper review into Ontario was minimal and there is no
evidence that Paulsson has suffered significant damages in Ontario.
[7]

I agree; this factor favours the applicants’ position.

[
34
]

Paulsson had been looking for an
academic or teaching positions for four years before this review was published.
No prospective employer came forward to suggest that the review influenced any
hiring decision that might support a damages claim. Indeed, the evidence
establishes that at least one other academic criticized Paulsson’s book in much
the same was as Cooper had. Reputational damage, if any, may have come from the
Ontario academic rather than from Cooper’s words.

The Connection Between the Forum and the
Defendants

[
35
]

The applicants clearly have no
connection to Ontario other than allowing 81 copies of the Slavic Review to be
distributed to two dozen libraries in the province. The University did not
publish and did not control editorial content. The review was not available on
either applicant’s web site and could not have appeared in the academic review
site, JSTOR, when it was published and not until the following year at the
earliest.

[
36
]

There is no evidence that anyone
ever read the review in Ontario or that Paulsson sustained significant damages
in Ontario as the result of anyone reading the review. There is no fair basis
upon which to conclude that the applicants could or should have assumed that by
allowing the 81 copies to be distributed into Ontario, Paulsson would suffer
damages.

[
37
]

Paulsson’s book was published in
the UK at a time when he lived and worked there. The evidence does not support
a conclusion that applicants should have foreseen that he had returned to live
in Ontario or that their conduct would result in harm to him in Ontario.

[
38
]

This factor certainly favours the
applicants’ position.

Unfairness to the Defendants in Assuming
Jurisdiction

[
39
]

There may be a certain unfairness
to the applicants if this court assumes jurisdiction arising from the fact that
American law in defamation cases may favour defendants over foreign plaintiffs
or, in the case of the University, that Illinois law apparently requires such
cases to be addressed in the Court of Claims where quantum of damages is
capped. This said, however, neither side tendered expert evidence on the law of
any American jurisdiction in which this matter might be tried.

[
40
]

In Black
[8]
,
Belobaba J. clearly heard evidence from American legal experts. Absent such
evidence, I am not prepared to speculate on the law of a foreign jurisdiction.
As such, this issue is neutral.

Unfairness to the Plaintiff in Not
Assuming Jurisdiction

[
41
]

Paulsson insists that some
activities, by their very nature, involve a sufficient risk of harm to
extra-provincial parties that any unfairness in assuming jurisdiction is
mitigated or eliminated.
[9]

[
42
]

I reject the argument that because
Paulsson is unemployed, looking for work and owns no property in Ontario and is
up against a university “with vast resources”, his position under this point of
consideration is somehow advanced.

[
43
]

Quite apart from the fact that
there is no evidence of the resources, vast or otherwise, owned by the
university, the financial well being of litigants before this court is simply
irrelevant to the determination of this factor. Another neutral outcome.

[
44
]

In any event, this factor only
comes into play where there is otherwise a real and substantial connection with
the action.
[10]

The Involvement of Other Parties to the
Suit

[
45
]

Paulsson suggests that this too is
a neutral factor. At best, from his perspective, it is. In my view it should
not be ignored that there are no defendants from Ontario named in this action.
Each of the defendants hails from a different jurisdiction and none of them are
resident in any Canadian jurisdictions.  To this extent, this factor tends to
favour the applicants.

Court’s Willingness to Recognize and
Enforce an Extra-Provincial Judgment

[
46
]

We are here dealing with an
international and not an extra-provincial situation. The applicants assert that
under this factor the court should consider the interests of potential Ontario
defendants to claims of defamation made by persons residing outside of Ontario
in respect of activities of Ontario defendants that take place within Ontario.

[
47
]

The applicants add that if the
court finds that the real and substantial connection test has been satisfied,
then Ontario courts will have to enforce foreign judgments rendered on the same
jurisdictional basis against academic institutions in Ontario, which have
minimal involvement with academic journals, and against associations based in
Ontario that publish academic journals.

[
48
]

Paulsson argues that in defamation
cases, vindication of one's reputation is often as important as obtaining a
monetary award of damages. If the actions of a foreign defendant can reasonably
be foreseen to cause damage to an Ontario plaintiff resident in this province,
then this reciprocity factor becomes less important in the overall
jurisdictional analysis.
[11]

[
49
]

In this case, I am not persuaded
that the actions of the applicants could reasonably have been foreseen to cause
damages to Paulsson in Ontario and the balance on this factor therefore falls
to the applicants’ side of the ledger.

Whether the Case is Inter-Provincial or
International in Nature

[
50
]

The parties agree that the law is
clear on this factor and calls for caution “where the core of the action
involves foreign defendants” in which case “courts should be more wary of
assuming jurisdiction simply because there is a claim against a domestic
defendant”.
[12]

[
51
]

Here there is no domestic
defendant and the case for caution is therefore more compelling. This factor
clearly favours the applicants.

Comity and the Standards of Jurisdiction
Recognition and Enforcement Prevailing Elsewhere

[
52
]

Whether or under what
circumstances a foreign court would enforce an Ontario judgment on a
comparative jurisdictional basis is a matter that I simply cannot determine
upon the evidentiary record available on this application. As noted above, the
parties have not led expert evidence on matters of foreign law.

Conclusion on Jurisdiction

[
53
]

In
Hunt
,
[13]

La Forest J. stated that:

Whatever approach is used, the assumption of and the
discretion not to exercise jurisdiction must ultimately be guided by the
requirements of order and fairness, not a mechanical counting of contacts or
connections.

[
54
]

With that admonition in mind and
having reviewed the eight applicable factors, I cannot conclude that this court
has jurisdiction to hear this particular action. I must, therefore, find that a
real and substantial connection to Ontario has not been established and
jurisdiction can therefore not be assumed.

[
55
]

In my view, the matter of whether
Ontario is a convenient forum for the hearing of the matter does not arise
unless or until the court has determined that a real and substantial connection
exists between the subject matter of the action and the Province of Ontario. As
such, I do not need to determine any issue of convenient forum.

[
56
]

Nevertheless, lest I be incorrect
in my determination that there is no real and substantial connection to Ontario
in this matter, I have reviewed the available evidence in the context of the
factors applicable to the determination of whether Ontario is a convenient
forum and I must conclude that Ontario is not a convenient forum for this
action.

Convenience of the Forum

[
57
]

The factors to be and that I have considered
in determining whether Ontario is a convenient forum are detailed in Muscutt
[14]

as follows:

(a)

the location of the majority of the parties;

(b)

the location of key witnesses and evidence;

(c)

contract rule provisions that specify applicable law or a cord
jurisdiction;

(d)

the avoidance of multiplicity of proceedings;

(e)

the applicable law and its weight in comparison to the factual questions
to be decided;

(f)

geographical factor suggesting the natural forum; and

(g)

whether declining jurisdiction would deprive the plaintiff of a
legitimate juridical advantage available in the domestic court.

[
58
]

Paulsson accepts that the
determination of this issue involves the exercise of judicial discretion in the
application of the relevant factors to the available evidence upon this
application. He insists that the burden of proof should rest with the
applicants but as all parties except the plaintiff are located outside of
Ontario I prefer the approach stated by Arbour J. in
Frymer
[15]

that:

[W]hen the plaintiff chooses a forum in which
jurisdiction exists "as of right", in the sense that the defendants
is a resident of that jurisdiction, the defendants has the burden of showing
that another forum is the convenient one. If the plaintiff chooses to bring a
foreigner into the jurisdiction, typically in the case of service
ex juris,
the
burden will be on the plaintiff to establish that Ontario is the appropriate
forum if the choice of forum is challenged by the defendants.

[
59
]

In
Amchem
[16]
,
a more liberal view, one not necessarily dependent upon the status of the party
as plaintiff or defendant was stated by Sopinka J.:

The burden of proof should not play a significant
role in these matters as it only applies in cases in which the judge cannot
calm to a determinate decision on the basis of the material presented by the
parties.

[
60
]

In the instant case, I have no
difficulty coming to a determination on the basis of the material presented by
the parties. The onus of proof is therefore not a significant concern. In any
event, the applicants have persuaded me to their view that Ontario is not the
most appropriate forum for the action.

[
61
]

The majority of the parties reside
outside of Ontario. This is an action arising from a book review authored in
Australia and published in Massachusetts. The evidence establishes that few, if
any, Ontario-based witnesses may be called in support of the plaintiff's case
whereas all of the identified witnesses for the applicants reside outside of
Ontario.

[
62
]

There are no contractual revisions
that specify applicable law in this case.

[
63
]

There are no other proceedings
extant in other jurisdictions and none are completed.

[
64
]

There are no relevant geographical
factors that assist in determining the issue.

[
65
]

As indicated above, this court is
hampered in its consideration of any applicable foreign law and its weight in
comparison to the factual questions to be decided, by virtue of the fact that
expert evidence on American or other applicable foreign law was not placed
before the court on this application. Arguably, as the book review was
published in Illinois, the law of that State  may be applicable; certainly the
factual matters affecting the claims made against the applicants arise
principally outside Ontario given the very limited circulation of the review in
Ontario.

[
66
]

I cannot conclude that Paulsson
will be deprived of a legitimate juridical advantage if Ontario is not found to
be a convenient forum without reference to the law applicable in other relevant
jurisdictions. As the parties have determined to proceed without a complete
record, including expert evidence on foreign law, I cannot accept the position
espoused for Paulsson on this factor.

[
67
]

Also unnecessary to my
determination of the outcome of this application is an answer to the question
of whether this court is entitled to assume jurisdiction over the University in
light of the provisions of the
State Immunity Act.

[
68
]

To determine whether the
University is an agent of a foreign state, this court would require expert
evidence addressing the application of Illinois legislation and other laws to
the status and operations of the University.

[
69
]

In the University of Calgary case
[17]
,
counsel agreed that the determination of whether the defendant School of Mines
was an agency of the state of Colorado is determined by Canadian and not
American law. At paragraph 23, Kent J. stated that:

Whether or not a particular institution is an agency
of the government, however, depends upon the control which is exercised by the
government.

[
70
]

Then in paragraphs 30 and 34, he
stated:

It is clear that the important consideration is who
has day-to-day control and management of the institution. For educational
institutions, some of the indicia considered by the court are financial
accountability, appointment of board members and whether the government has any
direct role in the daily, routine governance of the institution….

The board has control and management of the
institution, it sets its own bylaws and regulations, it makes decisions like
setting the amount of tuition and the legislature has recognized in some
circumstances it may act independently, albeit without the aid of government
funds.

[
71
]

In the instant case, counsel do
not agree that the determination of whether the University is a State agency is
a matter to be determined solely on application of Canadian law. In any case,
the evidentiary foundation upon which to base a proper analysis of the
applicability of the
State Immunity Act
on this application is simply
inadequate.

Outcome

[
72
]

The application is granted and the
plaintiff’s action is hereby stayed against the defendants, other than Leo
Cooper.

[
73
]

The applicants shall recover costs
in any event of the cause, payable forthwith and fixed at $12,000.00 plus
disbursements and GST.

___________________________

Moore J.
